summary.text: For every prime \(p\ge5\), set \(n=p(p-2)\) and \(M=\frac{(p-1)(p-3)}2p+1\), so that \(T_{n-1}=pM\) and \(M\equiv1\pmod p\); the preceding block contains composite numbers \(px\) for \(M-p+3\le x\le M\), giving \(v_p(a(n-1))\ge p-1\). In the following block, the only multiples of \(p\) are \(p(M+j)\) for \(1\le j\le p-2\), each with valuation exactly one, so \(v_p(a(n))\le p-2\); hence divisibility fails for the unbounded indices arising from infinitely many primes.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
T_r=\frac{r(r+1)}2
\]
be the \(r\)-th triangular number. Thus the sequence in question is
\[
a(r)=\prod_{\substack{T_{r-1}<m\le T_r\\ m\text{ composite}}}m.
\]
We will construct infinitely many, indeed arbitrarily large, integers \(n>1\) such that \(a(n-1)\nmid a(n)\).

For a prime \(p\), write \(v_p(x)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in a positive integer \(x\). We use the elementary facts
\[
v_p(xy)=v_p(x)+v_p(y)
\]
and, consequently, if \(x\mid y\), then \(v_p(x)\le v_p(y)\). Therefore it is enough to find, for infinitely many \(n\), a prime \(p\) for which
\[
v_p(a(n-1))>v_p(a(n)).
\]

Fix a prime \(p\ge 5\), and define
\[
M=p\frac{(p-1)(p-3)}2+1,
\qquad
n=p(p-2).
\]
Because \(p\ge5\) is an odd prime, \((p-1)(p-3)\) is even, so \(M\) is an integer. Two simple properties of \(M\) will be important. First,
\[
M\equiv1\pmod p,
\]
so
\[
p\mid M-1.
\]
Second, \((p-1)(p-3)/2\ge1\), and hence \(M\ge p+1\), in particular \(M\ge p\).

The definitions have been chosen so that the common boundary between the blocks defining \(a(n-1)\) and \(a(n)\) is \(pM\). More precisely,
\[
T_{n-1}=\frac{n(n-1)}2=pM.
\]
To check this without suppressing any arithmetic, multiply both sides by \(2\). Since \(n=p(p-2)\),
\[
2T_{n-1}=p(p-2)\bigl(p(p-2)-1\bigr).
\]
On the other hand,
\[
2pM=p^2(p-1)(p-3)+2p.
\]
After factoring out \(p\), the required equality becomes
\[
(p-2)(p^2-2p-1)=p(p-1)(p-3)+2.
\]
Both sides expand to
\[
p^3-4p^2+3p+2,
\]
which proves the identity.

It follows that the block whose composite elements are multiplied to form \(a(n)\) is
\[
T_{n-1}+1,\ldots,T_n
 =pM+1,\ldots,pM+n.
\]
Indeed, \(T_n=T_{n-1}+n=pM+n\). Similarly, the preceding block, used for \(a(n-1)\), is
\[
T_{n-2}+1,\ldots,T_{n-1}
 =pM-n+2,\ldots,pM.
\]
Here we used
\[
T_{n-2}=T_{n-1}-(n-1)=pM-n+1.
\]
Thus
\[
a(n-1)=\prod_{\substack{pM-n+2\le m\le pM\\m\text{ composite}}}m,
\qquad
a(n)=\prod_{\substack{pM+1\le m\le pM+n\\m\text{ composite}}}m.
\]

We first obtain a lower bound for \(v_p(a(n-1))\). Consider the \(p-2\) integers
\[
x=M-p+3,M-p+4,\ldots,M
\]
and the corresponding multiples
\[
px.
\]
Every one of these multiples lies in the block for \(a(n-1)\). The upper bound \(px\le pM\) is immediate. For the lower bound, the smallest one is
\[
p(M-p+3)=pM-p^2+3p.
\]
Since \(n=p(p-2)=p^2-2p\), the lower endpoint of the block is
\[
pM-n+2=pM-p^2+2p+2.
\]
The difference between the proposed smallest multiple and this endpoint is
\[
(pM-p^2+3p)-(pM-p^2+2p+2)=p-2\ge0.
\]
Thus all the numbers \(px\) under consideration belong to the required interval.

They are also all composite. Indeed, since \(M\ge p\),
\[
x\ge M-p+3\ge3,
\]
and \(p\ge5\); hence \(px\) is a product of two integers greater than \(1\). Consequently every one of these \(p-2\) numbers actually occurs among the factors of \(a(n-1)\).

Each such number contributes
\[
v_p(px)=1+v_p(x)
\]
to the valuation of the product. The baseline contribution from the \(p-2\) numbers is therefore \(p-2\). There is at least one additional contribution: the integer \(x=M-1\) lies in the displayed range, since
\[
M-p+3\le M-1\le M
\]
for \(p\ge4\), and \(p\mid M-1\). Hence \(v_p(M-1)\ge1\). It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(a(n-1))
&\ge \sum_{x=M-p+3}^{M}v_p(px)\\
&=\sum_{x=M-p+3}^{M}\bigl(1+v_p(x)\bigr)\\
&\ge (p-2)+1=p-1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Notice that this is only a lower bound: there may be further composite multiples of \(p\) elsewhere in the preceding block, but they can only increase the valuation.

We now obtain an upper bound for \(v_p(a(n))\). Every integer in the full block for \(a(n)\) has a unique form
\[
pM+k,
\qquad 1\le k\le n=p(p-2).
\]
We claim that
\[
v_p(pM+k)=
\begin{cases}
1,&p\mid k,\\
0,&p\nmid k.
\end{cases}
\]

If \(p\nmid k\), then \(p\nmid pM+k\), because \(p\mid pM\); hence the valuation is \(0\).

Suppose instead that \(p\mid k\). Write \(k=pj\). The inequalities \(1\le k\le p(p-2)\) imply
\[
1\le j\le p-2.
\]
Then
\[
pM+k=p(M+j).
\]
Because \(M\equiv1\pmod p\),
\[
M+j\equiv j+1\pmod p.
\]
But \(1\le j\le p-2\), so
\[
2\le j+1\le p-1,
\]
and therefore \(p\nmid M+j\). Thus \(p\) divides \(pM+k\) exactly once, proving that its valuation is \(1\).

There are exactly \(p-2\) multiples of \(p\) among the integers \(k=1,\ldots,p(p-2)\), namely
\[
p,2p,\ldots,(p-2)p.
\]
The valuation of the product of every integer in the full block is consequently
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{p(p-2)}v_p(pM+k)=p-2.
\]
The number \(a(n)\) is obtained by omitting from this full block all integers that are not composite. Every valuation is nonnegative, so omitting factors cannot increase the sum of the valuations. Hence
\[
v_p(a(n))\le p-2.
\]
This remains true regardless of which of the numbers in the block are prime: the calculation over the full block supplies the required upper bound.

Combining the two estimates gives
\[
v_p(a(n-1))\ge p-1>p-2\ge v_p(a(n)).
\]
Therefore \(a(n-1)\) cannot divide \(a(n)\), since divisibility of positive integers would force the opposite inequality between their \(p\)-adic valuations.

We have proved that for every prime \(p\ge5\), the integer
\[
n=p(p-2)
\]
satisfies
\[
n>1
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
a(n-1)\nmid a(n).
\]
Finally, primes are arbitrarily large. Given any bound \(B\), choose a prime \(p\ge5\) with \(p>B\). Then
\[
n=p(p-2)\ge p>B,
\]
and the preceding argument shows that this \(n\) is exceptional. Thus the set
\[
\{n>1:a(n-1)\nmid a(n)\}
\]
is unbounded, and every finite set of natural numbers is bounded. The exceptional set is therefore infinite. This disproves the conjecture that only finitely many such integers \(n\) exist.
